_note: Trust is Verify: the vetting routes the identity service already answers (built), and the in-service monitoring the Full Scope adds — the gates and badge worked out on read, shift-start face match, the patient's QR check at the door, and complaints. The Trust Score's number never leaves this engine. Wave 2 contract; Wave 4 extends.

routes.summary: Face match at shift start, before going online.

request.why: The capture, held by the provider for the match and not by MyThuso.

refusals.statement: The face did not match, so you stay offline and the desk is told.
refusals.why: Account sharing is the biggest fraud vector in gig networks (§11).

withdrawn.why: It asked the nurse's phone for a reference to a liveness capture and answered as if a face had been matched, refusing only a mismatch. No identity provider is contracted, so nothing can match a face, and whether matching one is biometric information is the Information Officer's undecided D-3: a route that carries a capture reference is a route that assumes the answer. Version two takes nothing about a face, asks the face-match door, which answers not-integrated, records the shift as not matched and applies the dispatch rule in force.

routes.summary: A patient scans the lanyard QR at the door.

response.why: Whether it is the person expected.

refusals.statement: This is not the person expected. Do not open the door; the desk has been told.
refusals.why: A mismatch triggers an immediate SOS (§11).

withdrawn.why: A wrong code was answered as a refusal, and a refusal rolls back everything the handler started, so the mismatch event and the incident it should raise could never leave the engine. It had no expiry, no count of tries, no way for a patient to say the person at the door is not her nurse, and nothing of who the code belongs to beyond the badge. Version two answers a wrong code with the tries left, raises the mismatch when the tries run out, refuses an expired code, and hands the patient the name and badge to confirm on POST /v1/trust/door-verifications/{appointmentRef}/answer@1.

routes.summary: Make a complaint about a person, reviewed within 24 hours.

response.why: When it will have been reviewed.

refusals.statement: That person is not on the vetting register.
refusals.why: A complaint is about somebody Verify can review.

withdrawn.why: It published person.under_review@1 the moment a complaint arrived, which tells Care, Movement and Access that a nurse is under review before anybody has read a word, and invites a dispatch engine to act on a complaint nobody decided. That is the weight nobody decided in another form. It also carried no visit, no account of what happened and no way to say when the review is due under the window in force. Version two records the complaint, publishes trust.complaint.received@1 to Core alone with the review deadline, and changes nothing about the nurse.

routes.summary: A nurse starts her shift. The face-match door is asked and answers not-integrated, so the shift is recorded as not matched and the dispatch rule in force decides whether she is offered work.

response.why: The shift start, in Verify's own store.
What the face-match door answered: not-integrated, while no provider is contracted. Never matched without one.
Whether she may be offered work from this shift, under the dispatch rule in force when it started.
The rule that decided it, an allowed value of the unmatched-shift-start-dispatch setting.
The settings version the shift started under, which it keeps.

refusals.statement: A shift start carries nothing about a face. This one sent something else, and it was refused unread.
refusals.why: No photograph, template, embedding or capture reference is taken while D-3 is undecided, and a field a phone sends beside the start is where one would arrive. It is refused rather than ignored, because an ignored field has still been received.

refusals.statement: A shift is started by a person the engine can identify.
refusals.why: A shift start is about one nurse. One the runtime cannot tell apart from another would be recorded against nobody.

refusals.statement: You are not on the vetting register.
refusals.why: Only somebody Verify vets starts a shift it records.

refusals.statement: You have no current verification, so a shift cannot start. Your vetting status says why.
refusals.why: No Trust Score, no dispatch. A shift started past a failing gate would put somebody on the desk's board who may not work.

refusals.why: The code says who is at the door. A code for nobody in particular proves nothing to the person opening it.

refusals.statement: You have no current verification, so there is no door code to show. Speak to the desk.
refusals.why: A patient told a code matches is told she can open the door. A nurse without a current badge may not be there.

refusals.statement: The patient has already checked who is at the door for this visit.
refusals.why: A new code after the check is finished is a second check nobody asked for, and a way to reopen a mismatch the desk has already been told about.

routes.emitsNoneBecause: A code is shown on the nurse's own phone and no engine acts on one being shown. What happens at the door is published when the patient answers.

routes.summary: A patient types the code the person at the door shows. A match hands her the nurse's name and badge to confirm; a miss says how many tries are left, and the last one tells the desk.

request.why: The visit the patient is expecting.
The digits the person at the door showed.

response.why: Whether the digits are the code shown for this visit.
How many wrong tries remain before the desk is told. A count of tries and nothing about the nurse.
The name of the nurse the code belongs to, when it matched.
Her badge tier id from packages/catalog/trust.json, when it matched and she holds a current one. Never a score.
True when this was the last try, so the desk has been told and an incident raised.

refusals.statement: No door code has been shown for this visit. Ask the person at the door to show one, or say they are not your nurse.
refusals.why: A code typed against a visit nobody has shown one for is a guess, and is refused rather than counted as a try.

refusals.statement: That code has expired. Ask her to show a new one.
refusals.why: An expired code is not a mismatch: nothing about the person has changed, only the time. It is not counted as a try and the desk is not told.

refusals.statement: This door check is finished. If you are worried about who is at your door, say they are not your nurse.
refusals.why: After a match is confirmed or the tries run out, another try is either a second answer to a question already answered or a guess after the desk was told.

routes.summary: The patient says whether the person at the door is her nurse. Yes needs a matched code; no is taken at any time, and raises a safety incident.

response.why: True when the patient confirmed a matched code.
True when the desk has been told and an incident raised.

refusals.statement: Say whether she is your nurse, or that she is not.
refusals.why: Two answers exist. Anything else is a guess at what the patient meant, at the moment a guess matters most.

refusals.statement: Type the code she shows before you say she is your nurse.
refusals.why: A yes without a matched code is a door opened on a name alone. A no needs no code, because a patient who sees a stranger should not have to ask one for digits.

refusals.statement: This door check is finished. If you are worried about who is at your door, say they are not your nurse.
refusals.why: A second yes to a check already answered adds nothing; a no is always taken, and is not refused by this.

response.why: When it will have been reviewed, under the window in force when it arrived.
That window, as the setting in force gave it.
The settings version the complaint keeps.

refusals.statement: That person is not on the vetting register.
refusals.why: A complaint is about somebody Verify can review.

refusals.statement: Choose what the complaint is about from the list.
refusals.why: A category is what a reviewer's queue and the nurse's notice carry, and a category typed freely is where a diagnosis would arrive in a header.

refusals.statement: Say what happened in your own words, in no more than the space the form gives.

refusals.statement: Nobody makes a complaint about themselves.

refusals.statement: A complaint carries what happened and nothing about what should happen to the nurse. It was refused unread.
refusals.why: A field beside the complaint — a score change, a suspension, a weight — is a decision made by the person complaining. The complaint rate's weight is null in packages/catalog/trust.json, and a complaint never changes a score by itself.

routes.emitsNoneBecause: No engine acts on a decided complaint. An upheld complaint reaches the Trust Score only through the complaint-rate input, whose weight nobody has decided, and a suspension is its own decision on the register, which publishes its own event.

Each setting: its key, type, unit, the value in force and the version that set it, its default and provenance, its limits, who may change it, what a change reaches, its guardrail, and its clinical review.

The roles that may change it, resolved from the contract and the settings in force.
What a change reaches, as a sentence.

The setting it changed.

The value after.
Why, as it was written.

refusals.statement: Only somebody who may change these settings reads them and who changed them.
refusals.why: The history names the people who changed how an engine behaves. It is read by the roles that may change it.

routes.summary: Change one Verify in service setting, with a reason, against the version in force. It applies to the shifts, door codes and complaints that start after it.

request.why: Chosen by the caller. The same key twice is the same change once, and the history gains one row.
The setting's key, from the settings block of the engine's own contract.
The new value, for a setting in minutes, a count, cents or a percentage.
The new value, for a setting that is on or off.
The new value, for a setting that is one of a few named choices.
The new wording, for a setting patients or nurses read.
The new roles, for a setting that names roles from packages/catalog/vetting.json.
The new rota, for a setting that is windows of a post, days and hours. A post, never a named person.
The new values, for a setting that is a list.
The new values, for a setting whose parts change together.
Why. Asked for by the handler rather than the binder, so that a change without one is refused in its own sentence rather than the general one for a missing field.
The settings version the admin was looking at. A change against an older one is refused.

response.why: When it took effect. Whatever started before it keeps the version it started under.

refusals.statement: Only the role a setting names changes it, and the change is recorded against a named person.
refusals.why: A setting decides how the platform treats people. The role or capability the setting names changes it, and a change is recorded against somebody who can be asked about it; everybody else only reads what is in force.

refusals.statement: There is no setting by that name.
refusals.why: An unknown setting is refused rather than stored, or the history fills with changes nothing reads.

refusals.statement: A change to a setting says why, or it is not made.
refusals.why: The history is read after something has gone wrong. A change with no reason is a number somebody moved.

refusals.statement: These settings changed after you opened them. Read what is in force now and decide against that.
refusals.why: Two admins changing one setting from screens opened at the same time would each overwrite a decision they never saw.

refusals.statement: That is not the kind of value this setting holds.
refusals.why: A word where a number belongs, or a list where one choice belongs, is a guess at what the admin meant, and a setting is never set by a guess.

refusals.statement: This setting is never nought or less, whatever its range says.
refusals.why: A wait of nothing, an offer that lapses as it is made and a fee of nothing are never what anybody meant. The range is a proposal and could be set wrongly; this refusal does not depend on it.

refusals.statement: Every role a setting names is a role on the vetting register.
refusals.why: A role the register does not hold is a gate nobody can be vetted through, which looks like a shortage rather than a mistake.

refusals.statement: That wording is longer than this setting allows.
refusals.why: The maximum is the space the words are read in. Wording that does not fit is cut off where somebody reads it.

refusals.statement: That wording drops a sentence this setting must always keep.
refusals.why: Some wording carries a promise that protects somebody. It may be reworded around that sentence and never without it.

refusals.statement: That rota leaves hours uncovered that must always have somebody on them.
refusals.why: A rota with a gap is an alert with nobody to go to, and nobody finds out until one arrives.

refusals.statement: That is outside what an admin may set for this setting.
refusals.why: The bounds, the allowed values and the allowed roles sit beside the default in the engine's contract. Moving a setting past them is a change to that contract, not a setting.

refusals.statement: That is already the value in force, so there is nothing to change.
refusals.why: A change that changes nothing is a row in the history saying something happened when nothing did.

routes.emitsNoneBecause: No engine acts on a settings change. The engine that owns a setting reads the value in force when it starts something, and the event contract refuses an event nobody subscribes to. A change is the row it appends to the engine's own history, which the read route returns.
